newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: China needs big effort to handle rising oil imports.
newsitem.headline: China needs big effort to handle rising oil imports.

text.p: China must speed up port modernisation, build an oil reserve and improve transport to cope with soaring crude oil imports, Chinese officials and analysts said on Tuesday.
These major tasks need to be achieved because China, armed with sizzling economic growth in the next five to 10 years, is emerging as one of the world's biggest oil importers, they said.
"Preparations must start as soon as possible to keep up with the rapid growth," said a senior official of state importer China Petrochemical Corp (Sinopec).
China expects to more than double imports of crude oil to 50 million tonnes a year by 2000, compared with an actual import of 22.6 million tonnes in 1996, according to Chinese state media.
Some analysts predicted even higher imports.

"If the progess of improvement is slow, when the huge oil imports arrive they won't be able to reach inland refineries within a resonable period of time and refineries can't handle them because facilities are not sophisticated enough," the Sinopec official said.
The government should coordinate related agencies to complete the tasks as they could not be done "single-handedly," said the official who asked not to be identified.
China's economy grew a sizzling 9.7 percent in 1996, exceeding an official target of 8.0 percent, and grew 9.4 percent in the first quarter of 1997.

With the world's biggest market of 1.2 billion people, China is expected to create a relaxed economic environment with Hong Kong returning to Chinese sovereignty at the end of June and the 15th Communist Party congress opening in October.

"China will become an oil import giant in coming years, so it must build up its own reserve system to make sure there won't be hectic price fluctuation," said Hu Angang, an energy expert at the Chinese Academy of Science.
Imported crude accounted for just five percent of China's annual oil consumption in 1995, said Hu, and the ratio would soar to 20-25 percent by the end of this century.

Chinese officials have called for a national oil reserve to avoid price volatility once China frees domestic crude prices within the next couple of years to allow prices to float at international market levels, analysts said.
"The system must be well regulated and safe," Hu said, adding that the government could even use its foreign reserves to build up an oil bank.

Over the past two decades, China has opened its markets to international trade, but only in recent years has it started to step into "crucial industries such as oil" on the international stage, Hu said.

Some oil traders said they doubted whether China would improve its inefficienct oil transportation, which sometimes caused port congestion and took a long time to get oil from its southeast coast to inland refineries.
"China's transportation system is one of the worst in Asia," said one trader in Singapore.

"Maybe China can improve its refinery facilities and build a national reserve system, but it could take them a long long time to upgrade the transportation because it's just too big," the trader said.
